title: Abstract
summary: Introduces the 2015 PLoS ONE study by Snir et al. on Ohalo II, a 23,000-year-old hunter-gatherer camp at the Sea of Galilee, Israel. Covers the analysis of about 150,000 plant remains showing gathering of over 140 species and grinding of wild wheat and barley. It identifies 13 current weed species mixed with wild emmer, barley, and oat seeds, presenting the earliest evidence of proto-weeds and a small-scale attempt at cultivating wild cereals, predating agriculture by about 11 millennia.

title: Introduction
summary: Explains that weeds emerged about 12,000 years ago with intentional cultivation in the Levant, using archaeobotanical evidence. Covers Holocene foraging-to-farming transition, niche construction by humans (fire, hunting, clearing), and synanthropic 'proto-weed' plants that thrived in disturbed habitats. Defines weeds, notes weeds in Neolithic assemblages indicate cultivation, stresses species-level identification, and presents Ohalo II Terminal Pleistocene evidence for the geographic origins of some Southwest Asian weeds.

title: Materials and Methods
summary: Describes Ohalo II, a Last Glacial Maximum (~23,000 years ago) settlement on the Sea of Galilee shore, Israel, later submerged. Covers its 1989-2001 excavations, six brush huts (four excavated, two sampled) with oval and kidney shapes, plant species used in construction, about 150,000 preserved seeds and fruits, flint and ground stone tools, faunal remains, beads, bone and wood objects, hearths, and an adult male grave.

title: Results and Discussion
key_items: The site of Ohalo II and its finds
summary: The text covers the Ohalo II site, a year-round settlement preserved under lake sediments. Its plant assemblage, over a third from grasses (wild emmer wheat, wild barley, wild oat), shows cereal processing evidence from a grinding slab with starch granules. Many plants were progenitors of later crops, indicating broad plant exploitation about 11,000 years before agriculture. Around 10.5% of charred seeds are proto-weeds, dominated by corn cleavers and darnel, suggesting their origin in human-made niches. Four weeds indicate a disturbed dump area. Wild barley and wheat rachises show high domestic-type scars, but the authors do not claim domestication. Flint sickle blades with polish suggest harvesting green-yellow cereals using composite tools, similar to Natufian methods about 10 millennia later.

title: Conclusions
summary: The text concludes that Ohalo II (about 23,000 years ago) shows small-scale trial cultivation of wild cereals, with no continuation afterward. Evidence includes many edible grasses (wild wheat, barley, oat), numerous proto-weeds, common domestic-type rachis scars, and the earliest sickle blades for planned harvesting. Domestication status is not claimed; the shift may have been rapid, within a few dozen generations. Findings predate Neolithic domestication by about 11,000 years, showing proto-weeds grew near camps and cultivated plots.

title: Ohalo II Supporting Information, Acknowledgments, and Author Contributions
summary: Supporting figures S1 and S2 describe seasonal availability of 68 bird and 101 plant species at Ohalo II, indicating year-round occupation, and show modern versus archaeological darnel (Lolium temulentum). Acknowledgments credit reviewers, lab and herbarium staff, and funders including the Israel Science Foundation and National Geographic Society. Author contributions list who designed experiments, analyzed data, and wrote the paper.

title: References
summary: A reference list (items 1–68) from the PLOS ONE article 'Origin of Cultivation and Proto-Weeds, Long Before Neolithic Farming' (2015). It cites works on crop domestication, plant invasiveness, niche construction, and weed ecology; archaeobotany and early agriculture in the Near East; the Ohalo II site (~23,000 years old) including plant, animal, fish, bird, and human remains, dating, and tools; Flora Palaestina and other botanical references; and wild cereal harvesting experiments, domestication rates, and wheat and barley domestication studies.
